description: Defining health, fitness and wellbeing and the physical, emotional and social benefits of sport.
content_html:
Defining Health, Fitness and Wellbeing

Three terms sit at the heart of this topic, and OCR expects you to define each precisely. Health is defined by the World Health Organisation as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing — not merely the absence of disease. A person can be healthy without being a high-level athlete, and an athlete can be medically fit yet psychologically or socially struggling. True health is multi-dimensional.

Fitness refers to the ability to meet the physical demands placed upon the body. A marathon runner is fit for her event; a weightlifter is fit for his. Fitness is always relative to the activity — there is no single universal measure. Wellbeing is the broader sense of being in a positive state — feeling satisfied, purposeful and capable across physical, emotional and social dimensions. Physical activity contributes to all three simultaneously, which is why it is one of the most powerful public health tools available.

Key Fact

OCR requires three distinct definitions: health (complete physical, mental and social wellbeing), fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) and wellbeing (positive state across physical, emotional and social dimensions). These are not the same thing — you can be fit but unhealthy, or healthy but not at peak fitness.

Physical Benefits of Participation

Regular physical activity produces a wide range of physical health benefits, many of which directly reduce the risk of the most serious long-term diseases. The OCR specification names seven physical outcomes you must know: reduced risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), improved blood pressure control, increased bone density, reduced risk of obesity, reduced risk of Type 2 diabetes, improved posture, and improved overall fitness.

Coronary heart disease: regular aerobic exercise strengthens the heart muscle, increases stroke volume and improves the elasticity of blood vessels. These adaptations reduce the risk of fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Over a lifetime of regular activity, the risk of a fatal heart attack is significantly reduced. Dame Sarah Storey, for example, has maintained exceptional cardiovascular health through decades of competitive cycling.

Blood pressure: regular activity keeps blood vessel walls flexible and reduces the resting demands on the heart, helping to maintain blood pressure within a healthy range. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a major risk factor for stroke and kidney disease, and inactivity is one of its primary causes.

Bone density and posture: weight-bearing exercise — running, gymnastics, team sport — stimulates bone remodelling, maintaining or increasing bone density and reducing the long-term risk of osteoporosis. Good muscular strength and balanced muscle development also support healthy posture, reducing the back pain and joint problems that arise from prolonged sitting or muscular imbalance.

Obesity and Type 2 diabetes: regular exercise burns energy and maintains muscle mass, supporting a healthy body composition and preventing obesity. Physical activity also improves the body’s sensitivity to insulin, meaning blood glucose is regulated more efficiently. Both obesity and Type 2 diabetes are strongly associated with inactivity, and both significantly increase the risk of further cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

Emotional Benefits of Participation

OCR specifically names three emotional benefits: improved self-esteem and confidence, better stress management, and positive body image. These are not optional extras — they carry equal mark-scheme weight to physical benefits in extended-response questions.

Self-esteem and confidence: achieving a personal best, mastering a new skill or winning a competition builds self-esteem. The process of setting a goal, training towards it and succeeding creates a sense of personal effectiveness that transfers into other areas of life. For young people in particular, sporting achievement can become a foundation for confidence in school, relationships and future careers.

Stress management: moderate to vigorous exercise triggers the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of calm and happiness, and endorphins, natural pain-relieving chemicals that produce a sense of euphoria. The neurological effect is a measurable reduction in perceived stress and anxiety. Regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol (the stress hormone) levels and a faster physiological return to calm after stressful events.

Body image: physical activity improves body composition and physical capability, both of which contribute to a more positive body image. This is particularly significant for adolescents, for whom body image is a major determinant of self-worth. Sport provides an experience of the body as something capable and powerful, rather than something purely aesthetic.

Stress is the body’s physiological response to a perceived threat or challenge. When stressed, the hypothalamus activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, preparing the body for action. Chronically elevated stress hormones damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

Exercise provides the body with a legitimate outlet for this physiological state. A run or a football training session allows the body to use the elevated heart rate and glucose productively. After exercise, serotonin and endorphin levels remain elevated for several hours, creating a period of improved mood and reduced anxiety. Over time, regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol levels. This is why physical activity is increasingly recommended by mental health professionals as a first-line intervention for mild anxiety.

Social Benefits of Participation

OCR names three social benefits: the development of friendship, a sense of belonging to a group, and the reduction of loneliness. These are genuine, evidenced outcomes of regular participation and are especially important for specific age groups.

Team sport and group exercise demand cooperation and communication. Playing in a netball team, a rowing eight or a football squad requires trust, shared responsibility and collective problem-solving. These interpersonal skills transfer directly to workplaces and communities. For children and young people, regular team sport is one of the most effective ways of developing the social skills that underpin healthy adult relationships.

Participation also creates structured social contexts where friendships form more easily. For individuals who are isolated — whether through disability, life transitions or mental health difficulties — joining a sports club can directly address loneliness. The shared purpose and regular contact of a club or team provide exactly the conditions in which new social bonds develop. For older adults, group exercise classes and walking clubs perform the same function, reducing social isolation and the health consequences that accompany it.

OCR explicitly requires you to “apply the above to different age groups”. This means you should be able to discuss how the benefits differ across children, young people, adults and older adults. For children: skill development, bone density, socialisation through team sport, building lifelong habits. For young people: stress management, body image, self-esteem, social belonging. For adults: CHD prevention, stress relief, maintaining healthy weight, social connection. For older adults: bone density maintenance (reducing osteoporosis risk), managing Type 2 diabetes, reducing loneliness, maintaining mobility and posture. In an extended-response question, referencing a specific age group with an example will push an answer from Secure to Mastering.

Key Fact

OCR’s named physical benefits: reduced CHD, improved blood pressure, increased bone density, reduced obesity risk, reduced Type 2 diabetes risk, improved posture, improved fitness. Emotional benefits: self-esteem/confidence, stress management, positive body image. Social benefits: friendship, belonging to a group, reduced loneliness. All 13 outcomes are examinable.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on wellbeing extended-response questions is writing only about physical benefits. OCR’s mark scheme distributes points across all three dimensions: physical, emotional and social. Structure your answer in three clear sections and aim for at least two named benefits per dimension. For a 3 marks — Calculate from Data question, always show your working, state the unit, and make a clear interpretive statement — quoting figures without explaining what they show earns only partial credit. On an 8 marks — Evaluate, OCR rewards (a) range of points across all three dimensions, (b) a balanced argument (sport improves wellbeing and the argument that these improvements vary by age group or type of activity), and (c) consistent sporting application. Use a “For X… However Y…” structure with a named sporting example anchored to each side.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Physical activity produces seven named physical health benefits (including CHD prevention, improved bone density, reduced obesity and Type 2 diabetes risk) alongside three emotional benefits (self-esteem, stress management, body image) and three social benefits (friendship, belonging, reduced loneliness).
  • The three dimensions are interconnected: improved physical health supports positive emotional wellbeing, and social participation through sport reinforces both. Addressing all three in exam answers is essential for higher marks.
  • OCR expects you to apply benefits to specific age groups: bone density matters most for children and older adults; stress management is especially relevant for young people; loneliness reduction is particularly significant for older adults.

practice_questions.text: Identify one emotional benefit of regular participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: improved self-esteem or confidence; better stress management; more positive body image. Accept precise or descriptive answers.

1 mark for a basic definition: a positive state across physical, emotional and social dimensions / feeling satisfied and capable. 1 mark for development: includes both the absence of illness and the presence of positive functioning across all three health dimensions; or gives an example distinguishing wellbeing from mere fitness (e.g. a person can be physically fit yet have poor emotional wellbeing if they suffer from anxiety or low self-esteem).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows participation rates and self-reported wellbeing scores for three groups of adults at a local sports centre.

Group | Weeks of exercise per year | Mean wellbeing score (out of 10)
A (0–5 weeks) | 3 weeks | 4.7
B (20–30 weeks) | 25 weeks | 6.9
C (40+ weeks) | 48 weeks | 8.2

Calculate the difference in mean wellbeing score between Group A and Group C, and suggest what this tells us about the relationship between exercise and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: 8.2 - 4.7 = 3.5 points (accept 3.5). 1 mark for showing working and stating the unit (points on the wellbeing scale). 1 mark for a valid inference: the 3.5-point difference in wellbeing scores suggests that higher levels of regular exercise are associated with substantially greater wellbeing, indicating a positive relationship between frequency of participation and wellbeing.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the bone density measurements (g/cm²) of two groups of 65-year-old women: those who have exercised regularly for 20 years and those who have not.

Group | Mean bone density (g/cm²)
Active (regular exercise) | 1.08
Inactive (little or no exercise) | 0.79

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of regular exercise on bone density in older women.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that active women have higher mean bone density than inactive women (1.08 vs 0.79 g/cm²). 1 mark for quoting both figures to support the comparison. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone remodelling, maintaining or increasing density over time. 1 mark for the health implication: the 0.29 g/cm² difference suggests regular exercise significantly reduces the risk of osteoporosis and fractures in older adults.

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular participation in team sport can improve both emotional and social wellbeing for a 14-year-old.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an emotional benefit (improved self-esteem/confidence). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (achieving a goal or developing a skill in team sport builds self-efficacy; exercise releases serotonin, reducing stress and anxiety). 1 mark for identifying a social benefit (making friends; sense of belonging to a group). 1 mark for linking to the 14-year-old context (adolescence is a period when peer relationships and self-image are especially important; team sport provides structured social contact that reduces loneliness and builds communication skills).

practice_questions.text: A health promotion officer argues that regular physical activity is the single most important factor in improving the wellbeing of older adults aged 65 and over. Evaluate this claim, considering physical, emotional and social wellbeing benefits.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): presents a balanced, sustained evaluation with points across all three wellbeing dimensions applied specifically to older adults; argues the case for physical activity (CHD prevention, bone density maintenance, reduced Type 2 diabetes risk, stress reduction, reduced loneliness through group exercise); presents a counter-argument with development (diet, social support networks, healthcare access also contribute to wellbeing; not all older adults can participate in exercise due to disability or chronic illness; some emotional wellbeing issues require professional intervention beyond exercise); reaches a justified conclusion about whether physical activity is the single most important factor. Sporting examples for this age group (walking groups, yoga, bowls, swimming) anchored throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): all three dimensions covered; case for physical activity and at least one counter-argument; sporting context mostly present; conclusion present.

Developing (3-4 marks): physical and one other dimension; some points about physical activity benefits; limited balance or counter-argument; conclusion may be present but not fully justified.

Emerging (1-2 marks): basic points about exercise being good for health; one-dimensional; no evaluation of relative importance.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an emotional benefit of regular physical activity named by OCR?
Which term describes a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of illness?
Regular weight-bearing exercise helps to maintain or increase _____ density, reducing the long-term risk of osteoporosis.
Exercise releases _____, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of happiness and reduced stress.
Match each wellbeing dimension to its named OCR benefit from physical activity:
right: Reduced risk of coronary heart disease and Type 2 diabetes
Improved self-esteem and better stress management
Development of friendship and sense of belonging to a group

flashcard_questions.q: What is the OCR definition of health?
flashcard_questions.a: A state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of illness.
The ability to meet the demands of the environment, including the physical demands of sport.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the seven physical benefits of regular exercise listed by OCR.
flashcard_questions.a: Reduced CHD, improved blood pressure, increased bone density, reduced obesity, reduced Type 2 diabetes, improved posture, improved fitness.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three emotional benefits of regular exercise listed by OCR.
flashcard_questions.a: Improved self-esteem/confidence, better stress management, more positive body image.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three social benefits of regular exercise listed by OCR.
flashcard_questions.a: Friendship, belonging to a group, reduced loneliness.
Achieving goals and mastering skills builds self-efficacy — confidence in one's own capabilities.

flashcard_questions.q: What is serotonin and why is it relevant to emotional wellbeing?
flashcard_questions.a: A neurotransmitter released during exercise that promotes feelings of happiness, calm and reduced stress.

flashcard_questions.q: How does team sport reduce loneliness?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides structured social contact and shared purpose, making it easier to form friendships.
Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty deposits, restricting blood flow and risking heart attack.

flashcard_questions.q: How does regular exercise reduce the risk of Type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: It improves insulin sensitivity, helping the body regulate blood glucose more efficiently.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is bone density especially important for older adults?
flashcard_questions.a: Weight-bearing exercise maintains bone density, reducing the risk of osteoporosis and fractures.
Working jointly with others towards a shared goal, adjusting individual behaviour to serve the team.

glossary_terms.definition: A state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of illness or disease.
The ability to meet the demands of the environment, including the physical demands of sport and exercise.
A state of positive physical, emotional and social health, where an individual functions effectively and feels satisfied with life.
A disease in which arteries supplying the heart muscle become narrowed by fatty deposits, restricting blood flow and potentially causing a heart attack.
A person's sense of their own value and capability, which physical activity can enhance through achievement and improved physical self-perception.
A neurotransmitter released during exercise that contributes to feelings of happiness, calm and wellbeing.
Working jointly with others towards a shared goal, adjusting individual behaviour to serve the team.
Persistently high blood pressure in the arteries, which increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

hero_image_caption: Regular participation in sport and physical activity supports physical, emotional and social wellbeing at every age.
